sections.html: Serrasalmus humeralis grows about 20 cm long. It belongs to the group of fin-eating piranhas, which are best kept individually in the aquarium on a long-term basis, if one wants undamaged specimens.

Valenciennes was the first descriptor in 1850, but there is no question that he had received the type specimen, for which he states "Amazon" as the type locality, from Castelnau. Castelnau corrected the type locality to "Araguaia" in 1855. It must therefore be assumed that S. humeralis is found in the Tocantins system.

For unpredictable reasons, piranhas of the fin-eating behaviour type – often after months of living together – single out and mob an individual of the group. The mobbed individual becomes marked with a bite mark directly before the dorsal fin. Usually the mobbed fish is eaten after some days by the remaining group, independently of the available food supply. Attempting group keeping requires very big aquariums; in tanks under 150 cm length, such attempts are hopeless from the outset.

The identification of many piranha species is difficult. Serrasalmus humeralis is one of the earliest described piranha species and therefore has many taxonomic problems. Valenciennes' description provided no picture; Castelnau made up for this in 1855. Castelnau's drawing is very true to detail. The piranhas imported from the Tocantins as Serrasalmus humeralis correspond in all essential characteristics (shoulder spot, caudal fin pattern, body shape, coloration) to Castelnau's illustration, but have so far been identified in aquarium and scientific literature as S. eigenmanni. The latter species was described in 1929 on the basis of a specimen from Guyana. If S. humeralis and S. eigenmanni are identical, the valid name would be S. humeralis. However, both species are currently assumed to be valid and only very similar.
